claim: Opisthorchiasis is an overlooked danger to Southeast Asia.
source: Opisthorchiasis is an overlooked danger to Southeast Asia.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that characterizes the disease status in the region.

claim: High-resolution disease risk maps are critical but have not been available for Southeast Asia.
source: High-resolution disease risk maps are critical but have not been available for Southeast Asia.
evidence: This statement in the abstract identifies a gap in available resources.

claim: A total of 12.39 million (95% Bayesian credible intervals [BCI]: 10.10–15.06) people were estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018 in four major endemic countries (i.e., Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam).
source: Even though the overall population-adjusted estimated prevalence presented a trend down, a total of 12.39 million (95% Bayesian credible intervals [BCI]: 10.10–15.06) people were estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018 in four major endemic countries (i.e., Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam), highlighting the public health importance of the disease in the study region.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate derived from the model-based analysis presented in the study.

claim: The overall population-adjusted estimated prevalence presented a trend down.
source: Even though the overall population-adjusted estimated prevalence presented a trend down, a total of 12.39 million (95% Bayesian credible intervals [BCI]: 10.10–15.06) people were estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018 in four major endemic countries (i.e., Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam), highlighting the public health importance of the disease in the study region.
evidence: This statement is supported by temporal analysis of prevalence data in the study.

claim: 20 diseases have been listed as NTDs.
source: To date, 20 diseases have been listed as NTDs, and opisthorchiasis is under the umbrella of food-borne trematodiasis (Ogorodova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a factual statement about WHO classification, supported by a citation.

claim: Opisthorchiasis is under the umbrella of food-borne trematodiasis.
source: To date, 20 diseases have been listed as NTDs, and opisthorchiasis is under the umbrella of food-borne trematodiasis (Ogorodova et al., 2015).
evidence: This classification is supported by a citation to Ogorodova et al., 2015.

claim: Two species of opisthorchiasis are of public health significance: Opisthorchis felineus (O. felineus), endemic in eastern Europe and Russia, and Opithorchis viverrini (O. viverrini), endemic in Southeast Asian countries.
source: Two species of opisthorchiasis are of public health significance, that is, Opisthorchis felineus (O. felineus), endemic in eastern Europe and Russia, and Opithorchis viverrini (O. viverrini), endemic in Southeast Asian countries (Petney et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement about species and their geographic distribution is supported by citation.

claim: The overall disease burden due to opisthorchiasis was 188,346 disability-adjusting life years (DALYs) in 2010 according to WHO's conservative estimation.
source: According to WHO's conservative estimation, an overall disease burden due to opisthorchiasis was 188,346 disability-adjusting life years (DALYs) in 2010 (Havelaar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from WHO cited through Havelaar et al., 2015.

claim: More than 99% of the burden worldwide attribute to O. viverrini infection in Southeast Asia.
source: Fürst and colleagues estimated that more than 99% of the burden worldwide attribute to O. viverrini infection in Southeast Asia (Fürst et al., 2012).
evidence: This estimate is attributed to Fürst et al., 2012.

claim: Five countries in Southeast Asia, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam, are endemic for opisthorchiasis, with an estimated 67.3 million people at risk.
source: Five countries in Southeast Asia, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam, are endemic for opisthorchiasis, with an estimated 67.3 million people at risk (Keiser and Utzinger, 2005).
evidence: This statement about endemic countries and population at risk is supported by citation.

claim: Chronic and repeated infection with O. viverrini leads to the development of fatal bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma).
source: It is well documented that chronic and repeated infection with O. viverrini leads to the development of fatal bile duct cancer (cholangiocarcinoma) (International Agency for Research on Cancer, 1994).
evidence: This causal relationship is supported by citation to IARC, 1994.

claim: The life cycle of O. viverrini involves freshwater snails of the genus Bithynia as the first intermediate host, and freshwater cyprinoid fish as the second intermediate host.
source: The life cycle of O. viverrini involves freshwater snails of the genus Bithynia as the first intermediate host, and freshwater cyprinoid fish as the second intermediate host.
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle, which is established knowledge in parasitology.

claim: Humans and other carnivores (e.g., cats and dogs), the final hosts, become infected by consuming raw or insufficiently cooked infected fish.
source: Humans and other carnivores (e.g., cats and dogs), the final hosts, become infected by consuming raw or insufficiently cooked infected fish (Andrews et al., 2008; Saijuntha et al., 2014).
evidence: This transmission route is supported by citations.

claim: Behavioral, environmental, and socioeconomic factors affect the transmission of O. viverrini.
source: Behavioral, environmental, and socioeconomic factors affect the transmission of O. viverrini (Grundy-Warr et al., 2012, Phimpraphai et al., 2017, Phimpraphai et al., 2018, Prueksapanich et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Raw or insufficiently cooked fish consumption is the cultural root in endemic countries, showing a strong relationship with the occurrence of the disease.
source: Raw or insufficiently cooked fish consumption is the cultural root in endemic countries, showing a strong relationship with the occurrence of the disease (Andrews et al., 2008; Grundy-Warr et al., 2012).
evidence: This behavioral factor is supported by citations.

claim: Poorly hygienic conditions increase the risk of infection, especially in areas practicing raw-fish-eating habit.
source: Poorly hygienic conditions increase the risk of infection, especially in areas practicing raw-fish-eating habit (Grundy-Warr et al., 2012).
evidence: This risk factor is supported by citation.

claim: Environmental and climatic factors, such as temperature, precipitation, and landscape, affecting either snail/fish population or growth of the parasites inside the intermediate hosts, can potentially influence the risk of human infection.
source: In addition, environmental and climatic factors, such as temperature, precipitation, and landscape, affecting either snail/fish population or growth of the parasites inside the intermediate hosts, can potentially influence the risk of human infection (Forrer et al., 2012; Suwannatrai et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement about environmental factors is supported by citations.

claim: Important control strategies of O. viverrini infection include preventive chemotherapy, health education, environmental modification, improving sanitation, as well as comprehensive approaches with combinations of the above.
source: Important control strategies of O. viverrini infection include preventive chemotherapy, health education, environmental modification, improving sanitation, as well as comprehensive approaches with combinations of the above (Saijuntha et al., 2014).
evidence: Control strategies are supported by citation.

claim: WHO recommends implementing preventive chemotherapy once a year or once every 2 years depending on the levels of prevalence in population, with complementary interventions such as health education and improvement of sanitation.
source: For purposes of public health control, WHO recommends implementing preventive chemotherapy once a year or once every 2 years depending on the levels of prevalence in population, with complementary interventions such as health education and improvement of sanitation (WHO, 2009).
evidence: WHO recommendations are cited.

claim: Thailand conducted national surveys for O. viverrini prevalence in 1981, 1991, 2001, 2009, and 2014.
source: Thailand conducted national surveys for O. viverrini prevalence in 1981, 1991, 2001, 2009, and 2014 (Echaubard et al., 2016; Suwannatrai et al., 2018), but the results of these surveys were presented at the province level, which is less informative for precisely targeting control interventions.
evidence: This historical information about surveys is supported by citations.

claim: The results of Thailand's national surveys were presented at the province level, which is less informative for precisely targeting control interventions.
source: Thailand conducted national surveys for O. viverrini prevalence in 1981, 1991, 2001, 2009, and 2014 (Echaubard et al., 2016; Suwannatrai et al., 2018), but the results of these surveys were presented at the province level, which is less informative for precisely targeting control interventions.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of province-level data.

claim: Suwannatrai and colleagues produced climatic suitability maps for O. viverrini in Thailand using the MaxEnt modeling approach based on climatic and O. viverrini presence data.
source: Suwannatrai and colleagues, based on climatic and O. viverrini presence data, produced climatic suitability maps for O. viverrini in Thailand using the MaxEnt modeling approach (Suwannatrai et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes previous work by Suwannatrai et al., 2017.

claim: The climatic suitability maps brought insights for identifying areas with a high probability of O. viverrini occurrence but did not provide direct information on prevalence of O. viverrini in population.
source: The maps brought insights for identifying areas with a high probability of O. viverrini occurrence; however, they did not provide direct information on prevalence of O. viverrini in population (Elith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous work, supported by citation.

claim: A risk map of O. viverrini infection in Champasack province of Lao PDR was presented by Forrer and colleagues.
source: A risk map of O. viverrini infection in Champasack province of Lao PDR was presented by Forrer and colleagues (Forrer et al., 2012).
evidence: This cites previous work by Forrer et al., 2012.

claim: High-resolution, model-based risk estimates of O. viverrini infection are unavailable in the whole endemic region of Southeast Asia.
source: To our knowledge, high-resolution, model-based risk estimates of O. viverrini infection are unavailable in the whole endemic region of Southeast Asia.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Bayesian geostatistical modeling is one of the most rigorous inferential approaches for high-resolution maps depicting the distribution of the disease risk.
source: Bayesian geostatistical modeling is one of the most rigorous inferential approaches for high-resolution maps depicting the distribution of the disease risk (Karagiannis-Voules et al., 2015).
evidence: This methodological statement is supported by citation.

claim: Geostatistical modeling relates geo-referenced disease data with potential influencing factors (e.g., socioeconomic and environmental factors) and estimates the infection risk in areas without observed data.
source: Geostatistical modeling relates geo-referenced disease data with potential influencing factors (e.g., socioeconomic and environmental factors) and estimates the infection risk in areas without observed data (Gelfand and Banerjee, 2017).
evidence: This describes the geostatistical modeling approach, supported by citation.

claim: Bayesian geostatistical joint modeling approaches provide a flexible framework for combining analysis of both point-referenced and area-aggregated data.
source: Bayesian geostatistical joint modeling approaches provide a flexible framework for combining analysis of both kinds of data (Moraga et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This methodological statement is supported by citations.

claim: A total of 2690 references were identified through systematically reviewing peer-review literatures.
source: A total of 2690 references were identified through systematically reviewing peer-review literatures, and 13 additional references were gathered from other sources.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the systematic review process.

claim: 13 additional references were gathered from other sources.
source: A total of 2690 references were identified through systematically reviewing peer-review literatures, and 13 additional references were gathered from other sources.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the systematic review process.

claim: 168 records were included, resulted in a total of 580 ADM1-level surveys in 174 areas, 210 ADM2-level surveys in 142 areas, 53 ADM3-level surveys in 51 areas, and 251 point-level surveys at 207 locations in five endemic countries.
source: According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 168 records were included, resulted in a total of 580 ADM1-level surveys in 174 areas, 210 ADM2-level surveys in 142 areas, 53 ADM3-level surveys in 51 areas, and 251 point-level surveys at 207 locations in five endemic countries (i.e., Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam) of Southeast Asia (Figure 1).
evidence: This summarizes the data collection results, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Around 70% and 15% of surveys were conducted in Thailand and Lao PDR, respectively.
source: Around 70% and 15% of surveys were conducted in Thailand and Lao PDR, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of survey distribution.

claim: Only two relevant records were obtained from Myanmar.
source: Only two relevant records were obtained from Myanmar.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the systematic review.

claim: Myanmar data was not included in the final geostatistical analysis to avoid large estimated errors.
source: To avoid large estimated errors, we did not include this data in the final geostatistical analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on data limitations.

claim: All surveys were conducted after 1970, with around 75% done after 1998.
source: All surveys were conducted after 1970, with around 75% done after 1998.
evidence: This is a temporal summary of the survey data.

claim: Most surveys (95%) are community based.
source: Most surveys (95%) are community based.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of survey types.

claim: Around 40% of surveys used the Kato–Katz technique for diagnosis, while another 42% did not specify diagnostic approaches.
source: Around 40% of surveys used the Kato–Katz technique for diagnosis, while another 42% did not specify diagnostic approaches.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of diagnostic methods used.

claim: Mean prevalence calculated directly from survey data was 16.74% across the study region.
source: Mean prevalence calculated directly from survey data was 16.74% across the study region.
evidence: This is a calculated statistic from the collected survey data.

claim: Around 70% of eligible literatures got a score equal or more than 7, indicating an overall good quality of eligible literatures in our study.
source: Around 70% of eligible literatures got a score equal or more than 7, indicating an overall good quality of eligible literatures in our study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quality assessment result with reference to a figure.

claim: Seven variables were selected for the final model through the Bayesian variable selection process.
source: Seven variables were selected for the final model through the Bayesian variable selection process (Table 2).
evidence: This is a methodological result with reference to Table 2.

claim: The infection risk was 2.61 (95% BCI: 2.10–3.42) times in the community as much as that in school-aged children.
source: The infection risk was 2.61 (95% BCI: 2.10–3.42) times in the community as much as that in school-aged children.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical model.

claim: Surveys using FECT (formalin-ethyl acetate concentration technique) as the diagnostic method showed a lower prevalence (OR 0.76, 95% BCI: 0.61–0.93) compared to that using Kato–Katz method.
source: Surveys using FECT (formalin-ethyl acetate concentration technique) as the diagnostic method showed a lower prevalence (OR 0.76, 95% BCI: 0.61–0.93) compared to that using Kato–Katz method, while no significant difference was found between Kato–Katz and the other diagnostic methods.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical model comparing diagnostic methods.

claim: No significant difference was found between Kato–Katz and the other diagnostic methods.
source: Surveys using FECT (formalin-ethyl acetate concentration technique) as the diagnostic method showed a lower prevalence (OR 0.76, 95% BCI: 0.61–0.93) compared to that using Kato–Katz method, while no significant difference was found between Kato–Katz and the other diagnostic methods.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the model.

claim: Human influence index was negatively correlated with the infection risk.
source: Human influence index and elevation were negatively correlated with the infection risk.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the model.

claim: Elevation was negatively correlated with the infection risk.
source: Human influence index and elevation were negatively correlated with the infection risk.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the model.

claim: Each unit increase of the HII index was associated with 0.01 (95% BCI: 0.003–0.02) decrease in the logit of the prevalence.
source: Each unit increase of the HII index was associated with 0.01 (95% BCI: 0.003–0.02) decrease in the logit of the prevalence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical model.

claim: Increase in 1 m in elevation was associated with the 0.003 (95% BCI: 0.001–0.005) decrease in the logit of the prevalence.
source: And increase in 1 m in elevation was associated with the 0.003 (95% BCI: 0.001–0.005) decrease in the logit of the prevalence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the statistical model.

claim: Model validation showed that the model was able to correctly estimate 79.61% of locations within the 95% BCI, indicating the model had a reasonable capacity of prediction accuracy.
source: Model validation showed that our model was able to correctly estimate 79.61% of locations within the 95% BCI, indicating the model had a reasonable capacity of prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is a validation result assessing model performance.

claim: The ME, MAE, and MSE were 0.24%, 9.06%, and 2.38%, respectively, in the final model.
source: The ME, MAE, and MSE were 0.24%, 9.06%, and 2.38%, respectively, in the final model, while they were −7.14%, 16.67%, and 5.09%, respectively, in the model only based on point-referenced data, suggesting that the performance of the final model was better than the model only based on point-referenced data.
evidence: These are validation metrics from the final model.

claim: The ME, MAE, and MSE were −7.14%, 16.67%, and 5.09%, respectively, in the model only based on point-referenced data.
source: The ME, MAE, and MSE were 0.24%, 9.06%, and 2.38%, respectively, in the final model, while they were −7.14%, 16.67%, and 5.09%, respectively, in the model only based on point-referenced data, suggesting that the performance of the final model was better than the model only based on point-referenced data.
evidence: These are validation metrics from the point-only model.

claim: The performance of the final model was better than the model only based on point-referenced data.
source: The ME, MAE, and MSE were 0.24%, 9.06%, and 2.38%, respectively, in the final model, while they were −7.14%, 16.67%, and 5.09%, respectively, in the model only based on point-referenced data, suggesting that the performance of the final model was better than the model only based on point-referenced data.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment based on validation metrics.

claim: Monte Carlo test for preferential sampling suggested that preferential sampling may exist for survey locations in one third (6/18) of the survey years.
source: On the other hand, Monte Carlo test for preferential sampling suggested that preferential sampling may exist for survey locations in one third (6/18) of the survey years (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the preferential sampling test.

claim: In 2018, the high infection risk (with prevalence >25%) was mainly estimated in regions of the southern, the central, and the north-central parts of Lao PDR, some areas in the east-central parts of Cambodia, and some areas of the northeastern and the northern parts of Thailand.
source: In 2018, the high infection risk (with prevalence >25%) was mainly estimated in regions of the southern, the central, and the north-central parts of Lao PDR, some areas in the east-central parts of Cambodia, and some areas of the northeastern and the northern parts of Thailand.
evidence: This is a spatial summary of model estimates for 2018.

claim: The southern part of Thailand, the northern part of Lao PDR, and the western part of Cambodia showed low risk estimates (with prevalence <5%) of O. viverrini infection.
source: The southern part of Thailand, the northern part of Lao PDR, and the western part of Cambodia showed low risk estimates (with prevalence <5%) of O. viverrini infection.
evidence: This is a spatial summary of model estimates.

claim: The central and several southern parts of Vietnam showed low to moderate risk of O. viverrini infection, while there was no evidence of O. viverrini in other parts of Vietnam.
source: The central and several southern parts of Vietnam showed low to moderate risk of O. viverrini infection, while there was no evidence of O. viverrini in other parts of Vietnam.
evidence: This is a spatial summary of model estimates for Vietnam.

claim: High estimation uncertainty was mainly present in the central part of Lao PDR, the northern and the eastern parts of Thailand, and the central part of Cambodia and Vietnam.
source: High estimation uncertainty was mainly present in the central part of Lao PDR, the northern and the eastern parts of Thailand, and the central part of Cambodia and Vietnam (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of model uncertainty with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Areas of northern Thailand showed an increasing trend in periods 1978–1988 and 1993–2003.
source: Areas of northern Thailand showed an increasing trend in periods 1978–1988 and 1993–2003, while most areas of the country presented a considerable decrease of infection risk after 2008.
evidence: This is a temporal trend identified from the model estimates.

claim: Most areas of Thailand presented a considerable decrease of infection risk after 2008.
source: Areas of northern Thailand showed an increasing trend in periods 1978–1988 and 1993–2003, while most areas of the country presented a considerable decrease of infection risk after 2008.
evidence: This is a temporal trend identified from the model estimates.

claim: The infection risk first increased and then decreased in areas of the north, the central, and the southern parts of Lao PDR and the central parts of Vietnam.
source: The infection risk first increased and then decreased in areas of the north, the central, and the southern parts of Lao PDR and the central parts of Vietnam.
evidence: This is a temporal trend identified from the model estimates.

claim: The east-central and western part of Cambodia showed an increasing trend in recent years.
source: The east-central and western part of Cambodia showed an increasing trend in recent years.
evidence: This is a temporal trend identified from the model estimates.

claim: The population-adjusted estimated prevalence over the study region presents a trend down after 1995.
source: The population-adjusted estimated prevalence over the study region presents a trend down after 1995 (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–9).
evidence: This is a temporal trend with reference to figures.

claim: The estimated prevalence in Thailand showed a fast decline after 1995.
source: At the country level, the estimated prevalence in Thailand showed a fast decline after 1995 and took on a gradually decreasing change in Cambodia.
evidence: This is a country-specific temporal trend from the model.

claim: The estimated prevalence in Cambodia took on a gradually decreasing change.
source: At the country level, the estimated prevalence in Thailand showed a fast decline after 1995 and took on a gradually decreasing change in Cambodia.
evidence: This is a country-specific temporal trend from the model.

claim: In Lao PDR, the overall prevalence maintained quite stable before 1990 and decreased slightly between 1990 and 1997, increased significantly after 1997, then decreased from 2006, and became stable after 2011.
source: In Lao PDR, the overall prevalence maintained quite stable before 1990 and decreased slightly between 1990 and 1997, increased significantly after 1997, then decreased from 2006, and became stable after 2011.
evidence: This is a detailed temporal trend for Lao PDR from the model.

claim: The prevalence is stable in Vietnam during the whole study period.
source: The prevalence is stable in Vietnam during the whole study period.
evidence: This is a temporal trend for Vietnam from the model.

claim: In 2018, the overall population-adjusted estimated prevalence of O. viverrini infection in the whole study region was 6.57% (95% BCI: 5.35–7.99%).
source: We estimated that in 2018, the overall population-adjusted estimated prevalence of O. viverrini infection in the whole study region was 6.57% (95% BCI: 5.35–7.99%), corresponding to 12.39 million (95% BCI: 10.10–15.06) infected individuals (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate for 2018 with reference to Table 3.

claim: Lao PDR showed the highest prevalence (35.21%, 95% BCI: 28.50–40.70%) in 2018.
source: Lao PDR showed the highest prevalence (35.21%, 95% BCI: 28.50–40.70%), followed by Thailand (9.71%, 95% BCI: 7.98–12.17%), Cambodia (6.15%, 95% BCI: 2.41–11.73%), and Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate for 2018.

claim: Thailand had a prevalence of 9.71% (95% BCI: 7.98–12.17%) in 2018.
source: Lao PDR showed the highest prevalence (35.21%, 95% BCI: 28.50–40.70%), followed by Thailand (9.71%, 95% BCI: 7.98–12.17%), Cambodia (6.15%, 95% BCI: 2.41–11.73%), and Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate for 2018.

claim: Cambodia had a prevalence of 6.15% (95% BCI: 2.41–11.73%) in 2018.
source: Lao PDR showed the highest prevalence (35.21%, 95% BCI: 28.50–40.70%), followed by Thailand (9.71%, 95% BCI: 7.98–12.17%), Cambodia (6.15%, 95% BCI: 2.41–11.73%), and Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate for 2018.

claim: Vietnam had a prevalence of 2.15% (95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%) in 2018.
source: Lao PDR showed the highest prevalence (35.21%, 95% BCI: 28.50–40.70%), followed by Thailand (9.71%, 95% BCI: 7.98–12.17%), Cambodia (6.15%, 95% BCI: 2.41–11.73%), and Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate for 2018.

claim: Thailand had the largest numbers of individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini (6.71 million, 95% BCI: 5.51–8.41) in 2018.
source: Thailand had the largest numbers of individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini (6.71 million, 95% BCI: 5.51–8.41), followed by Lao PDR (2.45 million, 95% BCI: 1.98–2.83), Vietnam (2.07 million, 95% BCI: 0.70–4.24), and Cambodia (1.00 million, 95% BCI: 0.39–1.90).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate of infected individuals for 2018.

claim: Lao PDR had 2.45 million (95% BCI: 1.98–2.83) individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018.
source: Thailand had the largest numbers of individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini (6.71 million, 95% BCI: 5.51–8.41), followed by Lao PDR (2.45 million, 95% BCI: 1.98–2.83), Vietnam (2.07 million, 95% BCI: 0.70–4.24), and Cambodia (1.00 million, 95% BCI: 0.39–1.90).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate of infected individuals for 2018.

claim: Vietnam had 2.07 million (95% BCI: 0.70–4.24) individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018.
source: Thailand had the largest numbers of individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini (6.71 million, 95% BCI: 5.51–8.41), followed by Lao PDR (2.45 million, 95% BCI: 1.98–2.83), Vietnam (2.07 million, 95% BCI: 0.70–4.24), and Cambodia (1.00 million, 95% BCI: 0.39–1.90).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate of infected individuals for 2018.

claim: Cambodia had 1.00 million (95% BCI: 0.39–1.90) individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini in 2018.
source: Thailand had the largest numbers of individuals estimated to be infected with O. viverrini (6.71 million, 95% BCI: 5.51–8.41), followed by Lao PDR (2.45 million, 95% BCI: 1.98–2.83), Vietnam (2.07 million, 95% BCI: 0.70–4.24), and Cambodia (1.00 million, 95% BCI: 0.39–1.90).
evidence: This is a country-specific estimate of infected individuals for 2018.

claim: There was an overall decrease of O. viverrini infection in Southeast Asia from 1995 onwards, which may be largely attributed to the decline of infection prevalence in Thailand.
source: Our estimates suggested that there was an overall decrease of O. viverrini infection in Southeast Asia from 1995 onwards, which may be largely attributed to the decline of infection prevalence in Thailand.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal trends observed in the data.

claim: The decline in Thailand was probably on account of the national opisthorchiasis control program launched by the Ministry of Public Health of Thailand from 1987.
source: This decline was probably on account of the national opisthorchiasis control program launched by the Ministry of Public Health of Thailand from 1987 (Jongsuksuntigul and Imsomboon, 2003; Jongsuksuntigul et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the decline, supported by citations.

claim: The high-resolution risk estimates in Thailand in 2018 showed similar pattern as the climatic suitability map provided by Suwannatral and colleagues.
source: Our high-resolution risk estimates in Thailand in 2018 showed similar pattern as the climatic suitability map provided by Suwannatral and colleagues (Suwannatrai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work.

claim: The national surveys in Thailand reported a prevalence of 8.7% and 5.2% in 2009 and 2014, respectively.
source: The national surveys in Thailand reported a prevalence of 8.7% and 5.2% in 2009 and 2014, respectively (MOPH, 2014; Wongsaroj et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites prevalence data from national surveys.

claim: The study estimated higher prevalence of 12.44% (95% BCI: 10.79–14.26%) and 9.34% (95% BCI: 7.88–11.02%) in 2009 and 2014, respectively, compared to national surveys in Thailand.
source: However, we estimated higher prevalence of 12.44% (95% BCI: 10.79–14.26%) and 9.34% (95% BCI: 7.88–11.02%) in 2009 and 2014, respectively.
evidence: This is a comparison between the study's estimates and national survey results.

claim: The overall prevalence of O. viverrini remained high (>20%) in Lao PDR during the study periods.
source: Our findings suggested that the overall prevalence of O. viverrini remained high (>20%) in Lao PDR during the study periods, consistent with conclusions drawn by Suwannatrai et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with previous work.

claim: A total number of 2.45 (95% BCI: 1.98–2.83) million people living in Lao PDR were estimated to be infected with O. viverrini, equivalent to that estimated by WHO in 2004.
source: We estimated that a total number of 2.45 (95% BCI: 1.98–2.83) million people living in Lao PDR were infected with O. viverrini, equivalent to that estimated by WHO in 2004 (WHO, 2002).
evidence: This compares the study's estimate with WHO's previous estimate.

claim: The risk mapping for Champasack province shares similarly risk map pattern produced by Forrer and colleagues.
source: Besides, our risk mapping for Champasack province shares similarly risk map pattern produced by Forrer and colleagues (Forrer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work.

claim: A national-scaled survey in Cambodia during the period 2006–2011 reported infection rate of 5.7%.
source: A national-scaled survey in Cambodia during the period 2006–2011 reported infection rate of 5.7% (Yong et al., 2014), lower than our estimation of 8.34% (95% BCI: 5.25–14.95%) in 2011.
evidence: This cites a previous survey result for comparison.

claim: The study estimated a prevalence of 8.34% (95% BCI: 5.25–14.95%) in Cambodia in 2011.
source: A national-scaled survey in Cambodia during the period 2006–2011 reported infection rate of 5.7% (Yong et al., 2014), lower than our estimation of 8.34% (95% BCI: 5.25–14.95%) in 2011.
evidence: This is the study's estimate for Cambodia in 2011.

claim: The national survey in Cambodia may underestimate the prevalence because more than 77% of participants were schoolchildren.
source: The former may underestimate the prevalence because more than 77% of participants were schoolchildren (Yong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference about potential bias in the national survey.

claim: A large survey in five provinces of Cambodia suggested a large intra-district variation, which makes the identification of endemic areas difficult.
source: Another large survey in five provinces of Cambodia suggested a large intra-district variation, which makes the identification of endemic areas difficult (Miyamoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites a finding from previous work about spatial variation.

claim: O. viverrini infection was underreported in Cambodia.
source: Indeed, O. viverrini infection was underreported in Cambodia (Khieu et al., 2019), and further point-referenced survey data are recommended for more confirmative results.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: An overall low prevalence was estimated in Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%) in 2018, corresponding to 2.07 million (95% BCI: 0.70–4.24 million) people infected.
source: Although an overall low prevalence was estimated in Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%) in 2018, it corresponds to 2.07 million (95% BCI: 0.70–4.24 million) people infected, comparable to the number in Lao PDR, mainly due to a larger population in Vietnam.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with interpretation.

claim: The number of infected people in Vietnam is comparable to the number in Lao PDR, mainly due to a larger population in Vietnam.
source: Although an overall low prevalence was estimated in Vietnam (2.15%, 95% BCI: 0.73–4.40%) in 2018, it corresponds to 2.07 million (95% BCI: 0.70–4.24 million) people infected, comparable to the number in Lao PDR, mainly due to a larger population in Vietnam.
evidence: This is an inference based on population size and prevalence.

claim: The risk mapping suggested moderate to high risk areas presented in central Vietnam, with a high risk in Phu Yen province for many years.
source: The risk mapping suggested moderate to high risk areas presented in central Vietnam, with a high risk in Phu Yen province for many years, particularly.
evidence: This is a spatial finding from the risk mapping.

claim: Phu Yen province is considered a 'hotspot' according to previous studies.
source: This agreed with previous studies considering the province a 'hotspot' (Doanh and Nawa, 2016).
evidence: This cites previous work that identified Phu Yen as a hotspot.

claim: There was no evidence of O. viverrini infection in the northern part of Vietnam.
source: Of note, even though there was no evidence of O. viverrini infection in the northern part of the country, Clonorchis sinensis, another important liver fluke species, is endemic in the region (Sithithaworn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the study about the absence of O. viverrini in northern Vietnam.

claim: Clonorchis sinensis, another important liver fluke species, is endemic in the northern region of Vietnam.
source: Of note, even though there was no evidence of O. viverrini infection in the northern part of the country, Clonorchis sinensis, another important liver fluke species, is endemic in the region (Sithithaworn et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: The infection risk was higher in the entire community than that in schoolchildren.
source: The infection risk was higher in the entire community than that in schoolchildren, consistent with multiple studies (Aung et al., 2017; Forrer et al., 2012; Miyamoto et al., 2014; Van De, 2004; Wongsaroj et al., 2014).
evidence: This finding is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A negative association was found between O. viverrini infection and elevation, suggesting the disease was more likely to occur in low altitude areas.
source: A negative association was found between O. viverrini infection and elevation, suggesting the disease was more likely to occur in low altitude areas, which was consistent with a previous study (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, consistent with previous work.

claim: HII showed a negative relationship with O. viverrini infection risk, indicating the disease was more likely to occur in areas with low levels of human activities.
source: HII, a measure of human direct influence on ecosystems (Sanderson et al., 2002), showed a negative relationship with O. viverrini infection risk, indicating the disease was more likely to occur in areas with low levels of human activities, which were often remote and economically underdeveloped.
evidence: This is a finding from the model with interpretation.

claim: Areas with low levels of human activities were often remote and economically underdeveloped.
source: HII, a measure of human direct influence on ecosystems (Sanderson et al., 2002), showed a negative relationship with O. viverrini infection risk, indicating the disease was more likely to occur in areas with low levels of human activities, which were often remote and economically underdeveloped.
evidence: This is an inference about the characteristics of areas with low HII.

claim: The habit of eating raw or insufficiently cooked fish was more common in rural areas than that in economically developed ones.
source: The habit of eating raw or insufficiently cooked fish was more common in rural areas than that in economically developed ones, which could partially explain our findings (Grundy-Warr et al., 2012, Keiser, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The culturally rooted habit of eating raw or insufficiently cooked fish is one of the determinants for human opisthorchiasis.
source: Indeed, this culturally rooted habit is one of the determinants for human opisthorchiasis (Kaewpitoon et al., 2008; Ziegler et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The estimate of the number of people infected with O. viverrini is higher than that of the previous study (12.39 million vs 8.6 million).
source: Our estimate of the number of people infected with O. viverrini is higher than that of the previous study (12.39 million vs 8.6 million [Qian and Zhou, 2019]) emphasizing the public health importance of this neglected disease in Southeast Asia, and suggesting that more effective control interventions should be conducted, particularly in the high risk areas.
evidence: This compares the study's estimate with a previous estimate.

claim: The national opisthorchiasis control program in Thailand applied interrelated approaches, including stool examination and treatment of positive cases, health education aiming at the promotion of cooked fish consumption, and environmental sanitation to improve hygienic defecation.
source: The national opisthorchiasis control program, supported by the government of Thailand, applied interrelated approaches, including stool examination and treatment of positive cases, health education aiming at the promotion of cooked fish consumption, and environmental sanitation to improve hygienic defecation (Jongsuksuntigul and Imsomboon, 2003).
evidence: This describes the control program in Thailand, supported by citation.

claim: A new strategy was developed by Sripa and colleagues using the EcoHealth approach with anthelminthic treatment, novel intensive health education on both communities and schools, ecosystem monitoring, and active participation of the community.
source: In addition, for areas with difficulties to reduce infection risk, a new strategy was developed by Sripa and colleagues, using the EcoHealth approach with anthelminthic treatment, novel intensive health education on both communities and schools, ecosystem monitoring, and active participation of the community (Sripa et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a new control strategy, supported by citation.

claim: The 'Lawa model' shows good effectiveness in Lawa Lake area, where the liver fluke was highly endemic.
source: This 'Lawa model' shows good effectiveness in Lawa Lake area, where the liver fluke was highly endemic (Sripa et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement about the effectiveness of the Lawa model is supported by citation.

claim: Common integrated control interventions are applicable not only for opisthorchiasis but also for other NTDs, such as soil-transmitted helminth infection and schistosomiasis, which are also prevalent in the study region.
source: Furthermore, common integrated control interventions (e.g., combination of preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel, improvement of sanitation and water sources, and health education) are applicable not only for opisthorchiasis but also for other NTDs, such as soil-transmitted helminth infection and schistosomiasis, which are also prevalent in the study region (Dunn et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement about integrated interventions is supported by citations.

claim: Implementation of integrated interventions in co-endemic areas could be cost-effective.
source: Implementation of such interventions in co-endemic areas could be cost-effective (Linehan et al., 2011; WHO, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Data collected from various sources might not be random and preferential sampling may exist.
source: We collected data from different sources, locations of which might not be random and preferential sampling may exist.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation.

claim: Preferential sampling might exist for survey locations in one third (6/18) of the survey years.
source: We performed a risk-preferential sampling test and the results showed that preferential sampling might exist for survey locations in one third (6/18) of the survey years (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the preferential sampling test.

claim: The impacts of preferential sampling might include improper variogram estimator, biased parameter estimation, and unreliable exposure surface estimates.
source: The corresponding impacts might include improper variogram estimator, biased parameter estimation, and unreliable exposure surface estimates (Diggle et al., 2010; Pati et al., 2011; Gelfand et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement about impacts of preferential sampling is supported by citations.

claim: The study did not take into account the preferential sampling issue for the final model to avoid a more complex model.
source: To avoid a more complex model, we did not take into account the preferential sampling issue for our final model, as the model validation showed a reasonable capacity of prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is a methodological decision explained by the authors.

claim: Sensitivity analysis showed that using the midpoint values of the intervals had little effects on the final results.
source: Sensitivity analysis showed that the using the midpoint values of the intervals had little effects on the final results (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis.

claim: Most of the surveys only reported raw prevalence or prevalence without clarifying whether weighting was applied.
source: However, most of the corresponding surveys were only reported raw prevalence or prevalence without clarifying whether weighting was applied.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the available data.

claim: The study calculated the estimated country- and provincial-level prevalence by averaging the estimated pixel-level prevalence weighted by population density.
source: On the other hand, as population density across the study region was different, we calculated the estimated country- and provincial-level prevalence by averaging the estimated pixel-level prevalence weighted by population density.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach for aggregating estimates.

claim: The study assumed similar proportions of age and gender in different surveys.
source: We assumed similar proportions of age and gender in different surveys, as most of which only reported prevalence aggregated by age and gender.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption due to data limitations.

claim: The analysis was based on survey data under different diagnostic methods.
source: Furthermore, our analysis was based on survey data under different diagnostic methods.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the data used.

claim: The sensitivity and specificity of the same diagnostic method may differ across studies.
source: The sensitivity and specificity of the same diagnostic method may differ across studies (Charoensuk et al., 2019; Laoprom et al., 2016; Sayasone et al., 2015), while different diagnostic methods may result in different results in the same survey.
evidence: This statement about diagnostic variability is supported by citations.

claim: Different diagnostic methods may result in different results in the same survey.
source: The sensitivity and specificity of the same diagnostic method may differ across studies (Charoensuk et al., 2019; Laoprom et al., 2016; Sayasone et al., 2015), while different diagnostic methods may result in different results in the same survey.
evidence: This is a statement about diagnostic method variability.

claim: The study assumed the same diagnostic method has similar sensitivity and specificity.
source: To partially taking into account the diversity of diagnostic methods, we assumed the same diagnostic method has similar sensitivity and specificity, and we considered the types of diagnostic methods as covariates in the model.
evidence: This is a methodological assumption.

claim: The odds of infection with FECT methods was significantly lower than that with Kato–Katz.
source: Results showed that the odds of infection with FECT methods was significantly lower than that with Kato–Katz, which was consistent with results found by Lovis et al., 2009.
evidence: This is a finding from the model, consistent with previous work.

claim: Most of the diagnostic methods in the surveys were based on fecal microscopic technique on eggs, which could not effectively distinguish between O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes of the family Heterophyidae.
source: In addition, most of the diagnostic methods in the surveys were based on fecal microscopic technique on eggs, which could not effectively distinguish between O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes of the family Heterophyidae (e.g., heterophyid and lecithodendriid) (Charoensuk et al., 2019, Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the diagnostic methods, supported by citations.

claim: The results may overestimate the O. viverrini infection risk in areas where heterophyid and lecithodendriid are endemic.
source: Thus, our results may overestimate the O. viverrini infection risk in areas where heterophyid and lecithodendriid are endemic, such as Phongsaly, Saravane, and Champasak provinces in Lao PDR (Sato et al., 2010, Chai et al., 2010; Chai et al., 2013), Nan and Lampang provinces in Thailand (Wijit et al., 2013), and Takeo province in Cambodia (Sohn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of potential overestimation due to diagnostic limitations, supported by citations.

claim: There is an urgent need for the application of more powerful diagnostic practices with higher sensitivity and specificity to better detect the true O. viverrini prevalence, such as PCR.
source: There is an urgent need for the application of more powerful diagnostic practices with higher sensitivity and specificity to better detect the true O. viverrini prevalence, such as PCR (Lovis et al., 2009, Lu et al., 2017, Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a recommendation supported by citations.

claim: O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes have similar treatment and prevention strategies.
source: Nevertheless, because of the similar treatment and the prevention strategies of O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes (Keiser and Utzinger, 2010), our risk mapping is valuable also for areas co-endemic with the above flukes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: The risk mapping is valuable also for areas co-endemic with O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes.
source: Nevertheless, because of the similar treatment and the prevention strategies of O. viverrini and minute intestinal flukes (Keiser and Utzinger, 2010), our risk mapping is valuable also for areas co-endemic with the above flukes.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the risk maps.

claim: More comprehensive epidemiological studies are urgently needed for endemic areas with scant survey data.
source: More comprehensive epidemiological studies are urgently needed for endemic areas with scant survey data.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on data gaps identified in the study.
